content:
Muslims often say that the Bible blames Eve for the fall and the Quran does not. Christian critics answer that the Quran took its stories of the prophets, Adam's among them, from Jewish and Christian sources.[1]

Both claims can be checked against the texts. Genesis 2 and 3 are one account, and the Quran tells the story across several passages, chiefly 2:30 to 39, 7:11 to 27 and 20:115 to 123. Each has to be read before the theology built on it.

This article aims to provide context to those claims, insha'Allah, in five differences between the two accounts. The Quran's own summary of the outcome frames them: "Then learnt Adam from his Lord words of inspiration, and his Lord Turned towards him; for He is Oft-Returning, Most Merciful" (2:37).[2]

In Genesis the serpent speaks first with the woman. "She took some of its fruit, and ate; and she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too" (Genesis 3:6).[3]

In the Quran Satan addresses the couple together. "Then began Satan to whisper suggestions to them", and "by deceit he brought about their fall" (7:20, 22). In another passage he speaks to Adam by name: "O Adam! shall I lead thee to the Tree of Eternity and to a kingdom that never decays?" (20:120).[2]

Genesis does not excuse Adam, who eats and is judged. The Quran gives the woman no first step to take alone, and no verse of it makes her the opening of the fall.

The Quran makes the act and the repentance joint. "They both ate of the tree", it says (20:121), and both pray: "Our Lord! We have wronged our own souls: If thou forgive us not and bestow not upon us Thy Mercy, we shall certainly be lost" (7:23).[2]

Genesis records a different scene. "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it," the man says, and the woman says, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate" (Genesis 3:12 to 13).[3] Each passes the blame on, and God judges all three.

Later Christian texts put the weight on the woman. "Adam wasn't deceived, but the woman, being deceived, has fallen into disobedience" (1 Timothy 2:14), and Sirach, which Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include, says: "From a woman was the beginning of sin; And because of her we all die" (25:24).[4] Romans puts it on the man: "sin entered into the world through one man" (5:12).[5]

Genesis tells of judgement, of God clothing the pair in "coats of animal skins" (3:21), and of the expulsion.[3] It records no prayer of repentance and no statement that God accepted one.

The Quran does both. Adam learns "words of inspiration" from his Lord, and his Lord turns to him (2:37). "His Lord chose him (for His Grace): He turned to him, and gave him Guidance" (20:122).[2]

That turn is the hinge of the Islamic account. Adam's sin is real, and it is forgiven before he leaves the Garden. His story establishes repentance as the first thing a human being learns from God.

Both accounts describe consequences. Genesis names toil and death: "the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life" (3:17).[3] The Quran sends the couple down to the earth, "your dwelling-place and your means of livelihood - for a time" (2:36).[2]

The difference lies in what follows. Paul makes Adam the one through whom sin and death enter the world and sets him against Christ, and the doctrine of original sin grew from that pairing.[5] The Quran moves from the descent straight to guidance: "if, as is sure, there comes to you Guidance from Me, whosoever follows My Guidance, will not lose his way, nor fall into misery" (20:123).[2] Human history becomes a history of revelation and of each person's test.

The Quran states the rule five times in near-identical words: "no bearer of burdens can bear the burden of another" (6:164; 17:15; 35:18; 39:7; 53:38).[6] Each person inherits a world shaped by earlier acts, and inherits no one's guilt.

The churches answer the question in different ways. The Catholic Catechism says original sin in Adam's descendants is no personal fault, while the Westminster Confession says the guilt of Adam's sin was "imputed" to his posterity.[7] We set out those positions in our article on original sin.

The Quran never names Adam's wife; the name Ḥawwāʾ comes from the hadith and later tradition. A report in al-Bukhari and Muslim says that "were it not for Eve, no woman would ever betray her husband".[8] The commentary of the Dorar al-Saniyya hadith encyclopedia explains that the betrayal meant is her failure to give sound counsel in the matter of the tree, and no betrayal of the marriage.[9]

The report speaks of a trait, and it lays no guilt on her daughters. The Quran's own account keeps the two together through every step: both are tempted, both eat, both confess, and both are forgiven.

The bottom line

Genesis and the Quran share the shape of the story: a command, a tempter, a disobedience and a descent from the Garden. They differ in five places. The Quran has Satan tempt both, holds both to account, records their repentance and God's acceptance of it, turns at once to guidance, and denies that the guilt passes on.

Genesis keeps Adam answerable, and it was later texts that put the weight on the woman. The Quran tells the story so that every reader learns what Adam learned: "Our Lord! We have wronged our own souls" (7:23).[2] We set out the other prophets the two books share in 6 prophets both books share. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. The second claim is the thesis of William St. Clair Tisdall, The Original Sources of the Qur'an (London: SPCK, 1905); the first is the comparison this article tests.
  2. Quran 2:36 to 37; 7:19 to 23; 20:115 to 123, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Genesis 3:1 to 24 (World English Bible).
  4. 1 Timothy 2:13 to 14; Sirach 25:24 (World English Bible).
  5. Romans 5:12 to 21 (World English Bible).
  6. Quran 6:164; 17:15; 35:18; 39:7; 53:38, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  7. Catechism of the Catholic Church, 404 to 405; Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), chapter 6, section 3.
  8. Sahih al-Bukhari 3330 and Sahih Muslim 1470, from Abu Hurayra (numbering of sunnah.com).
  9. Al-Mawsūʿa al-Ḥadīthiyya, Dorar al-Saniyya, commentary on the hadith, dorar.net/hadith/sharh/22159.
